\chapter{Dog and Cat}
\label{ch:hi-dog-and-cat}
\hlchaptermodality{23}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name a dog and a cat in Hindi and say honestly how far back each word can actually be traced.}

Trace \hi{बिल्ली} back through biḍālikā to biḍāla, then say out loud where the evidence stops being solid.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[kuttā]{\hi{कुत्ता} — a third mystery dog-word}

\label{lesson:HI-C23-kutta-billi}



\begin{quote}
Spanish has a mystery dog-word, and English/German another. Hindi genuinely gives you a \textbf{third}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — \hi{कुत्ता} — a third mystery, displacing Sanskrit's own PIE word}
Sanskrit's actual, \textbf{inherited} word for dog was \textbf{\hi{श्वान}} (\emph{śvān}) — the \textbf{exact same PIE root}, \emph{\textbf{*\'{k}won-}}, behind Latin's \emph{canis}, English's \emph{hound}, and German's \emph{Hund}. It's the \textbf{only} word for dog found in the Rigveda. But everyday Hindi doesn't use \emph{śvān} at all — the ordinary word is \textbf{\hi{कुत्ता}} (\emph{kuttā}), which traces through Prakrit to a Sanskrit form, \textbf{\hi{कुर्कुर}} (\emph{kurkura}). Its ultimate origin is honestly \textbf{unresolved} — serious proposals split between an \textbf{onomatopoeic} origin (imitating a dog's bark) and a \textbf{non-Indo-Aryan substrate} word borrowed from an unrelated language family, with no consensus on which is right. Either way, \emph{kuttā} quietly pushed \emph{śvān} into rare, formal, literary use — the \textbf{exact same shape of story} as Spanish's \emph{perro} displacing \emph{can}, and English's \emph{dog} displacing \emph{hound}. Three unrelated language families, three mystery words, all crowding out the same inherited PIE word for \textquotedblleft{}dog.\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}kuttā\textquotedblright{} — dog, genuinely uncertain origin, displacing Sanskrit's own śvān
  \item \textquotedblleft{}śvān\textquotedblright{} — the PIE-inherited word, now rare and formal
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was Sanskrit's actual inherited word for \textquotedblleft{}dog,\textquotedblright{} and what family does it belong to? (\textbf{\hi{श्वान}}, \emph{śvān} — same PIE root as Latin \emph{canis}, English \emph{hound}, German \emph{Hund}.) Does everyday Hindi use \emph{śvān}? (\textbf{No} — \emph{kuttā} displaced it, echoing Spanish's \emph{perro} and English's \emph{dog}.) Is \emph{kuttā}'s own origin settled? (\textbf{No} — genuinely disputed between an onomatopoeic origin and a non-Indo-Aryan substrate word.) Next: follow Hindi's cat-word into a probable fourth family.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[billī]{\hi{बिल्ली} — a probable fourth cat-word family}

\label{lesson:HI-C23-billi-history}



\begin{quote}
Hindi's dog-word joined three mysteries. Its cat-word probably opens a family separate from the widespread \emph{qiṭṭ/cattus/gato/chat/Katze} story.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know — The route into Hindi}
\textbf{\hi{बिल्ली}} (\emph{billī}, \textquotedblleft{}cat\textquotedblright{}) traces through Sauraseni Prakrit to Sanskrit \textbf{\hi{बिडालिका}} (\emph{biḍālikā}), a diminutive of \textbf{\hi{बिडाल}} (\emph{biḍāla}, \textquotedblleft{}cat\textquotedblright{}).

Be honest about the deeper step: most linguists consider \emph{biḍāla} a loanword \textbf{into Sanskrit from Dravidian}, but this is not universal. Some scholars are skeptical of the comparison; another serious proposal derives it from an unattested native compound, \emph{\textbf{vidāla}, \textquotedblleft{}that which tears apart small birds.\textquotedblright{}}

If the leading Dravidian account is right, \emph{billī} belongs to a probable fourth cat-word family. Arabic \emph{qiṭṭ}, Latin \emph{cattus}, Spanish \emph{gato}, French \emph{chat}, and German \emph{Katze} are usually linked to one Afro-Asiatic source; Hindi's word would instead descend from a word Sanskrit borrowed from Dravidian.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textquotedblleft{}billī\textquotedblright{} — cat
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \emph{biḍāla} $\to$ \emph{biḍālikā} $\to$ Prakrit $\to$ \emph{billī}
  \item \emph{Qualify:} \textquotedblleft{}probably Dravidian, not proven\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textbf{\hi{बिल्ली}} most likely come from? (\textbf{Dravidian}, via Sanskrit \emph{biḍāla}.) Is that universally agreed? (\textbf{No} — it is the leading account with serious alternatives.) Why is this a new cat-word family? (It is probably separate from the \emph{qiṭṭ/cattus} family.)
\end{tcolorbox}
